indicators.label: Mood
indicators.what_it_means: How you feel; it feeds the perception gap.
indicators.why_in_space: Isolation and distance from Earth weigh on behavioural health.

source.citation: NASA HRP — Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders

indicators.label: Blood pressure (systolic)
indicators.how_to_measure: With the cuff, at rest, after a few minutes sitting down.
indicators.what_it_means: The pressure of blood on the arteries; we follow it as a trend against your normal.
indicators.why_in_space: In microgravity, fluids shift towards the head, and blood pressure is usually lower than on Earth.

source.citation: NASA HRP — Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations

indicators.label: Blood pressure (diastolic)
indicators.how_to_measure: The second value shown by the cuff.
indicators.why_in_space: Its trend helps prepare for the return to gravity.

source.citation: Norsk et al. (2015), Fluid shifts, vasodilatation and ambulatory blood pressure reduction during long duration spaceflight, Journal of Physiology 593(3):573–584

indicators.label: Heart rate
indicators.how_to_measure: Count the beats at your wrist for 30 seconds and multiply by 2, at rest.
indicators.what_it_means: Your heart rhythm; a rise above your normal can signal tiredness or an infection.
indicators.why_in_space: At rest, heart rate does not usually rise in flight, so a sustained rise is a real signal.

source.citation: Alavi et al. (2022), Real-time alerting system for COVID-19 and other stress events using wearable data, Nature Medicine 28:175–184

indicators.label: Blood glucose
indicators.how_to_measure: With the glucose meter, in the morning, before eating.
indicators.what_it_means: Your blood sugar level; a general health indicator.
indicators.why_in_space: Long flights can reduce insulin sensitivity, and skipped meals unbalance it (weak evidence).

source.citation: Hughson et al. (2016), Increased postflight carotid artery stiffness and inflight insulin resistance resulting from 6-mo spaceflight in male and female astronauts, Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol 310(5):H628–H638

indicators.label: Temperature
indicators.how_to_measure: With the thermometer, at the same time every day.
indicators.what_it_means: A rise above your normal can signal an infection.
indicators.why_in_space: In a closed space, an infection can spread to the whole crew.

source.citation: Stahn et al. (2017), Increased core body temperature in astronauts during long-duration space missions, Scientific Reports 7:16180

indicators.label: Sleep
indicators.how_to_measure: Filled in automatically from the sleep sensor; you can correct it.
indicators.what_it_means: Little sleep for a few nights in a row lowers your attention without you noticing.
indicators.why_in_space: Astronauts sleep about 6 hours on average, because of light, noise and the schedule.

source.citation: Van Dongen et al. (2003), The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness, Sleep 26(2):117–126

indicators.label: Did you eat all your meals yesterday?
indicators.what_it_means: Skipped meals can explain unbalanced blood sugar or tiredness.
indicators.why_in_space: Exercise protects bones only together with enough energy intake.

source.citation: Smith et al. (2012), Benefits for bone from resistance exercise and nutrition in long-duration spaceflight, Journal of Bone and Mineral Research 27(9):1896–1906
